{{Short description|Class of "well-behaved" models in set theory}}

In [[model theory]], a mathematical discipline, a '''β-model''' (from the French "bon ordre", well-ordering<ref>C. Smoryński, "[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0049237X09701600 Nonstandard Models and Related Developments]" (p. 189). From ''Harvey Friedman's Research on the Foundations of Mathematics'' (1985), Studies in Logic and the Foundations of Mathematics vol. 117.</ref>) is a model that is correct about statements of the form "''X'' is [[well-ordered]]". The term was introduced by [[Andrzej Mostowski|Mostowski]] (1959)<ref name="AM">K. R. Apt, W. Marek, "[https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0003484374900011 Second-order Arithmetic and Some Related Topics]" (1973), p. 181</ref><ref>[[J.-Y. Girard]], ''Proof Theory and Logical Complexity'' (1987), Part III: &Pi;<sub>2</sub><sup>1</sup>-proof theory, p. 206</ref> as a strengthening of the notion of ω-model. In contrast to the notation for set-theoretic properties named by [[ordinal number|ordinal]]s, such as [[Indescribable cardinal|<math>\xi</math>-indescribability]], the letter β here is only denotational.

==In analysis==
β-models appear in the study of the [[reverse mathematics]] of subsystems of [[second-order arithmetic]]. In this context, a β-model of a subsystem of second-order arithmetic is a model ''M'' where for any [[Analytical hierarchy|Σ<sub>1</sub><sup>1</sup>]] formula <math>\phi</math> with parameters from ''M'', <math>(\omega,M,+,\times,0,1,<)\vDash\phi</math> iff <math>(\omega,\mathcal P(\omega),+,\times,0,1,<)\vDash\phi</math>.<ref name="Simpson2009">{{Cite book |last=Simpson |first=Stephen G. |authorlink = Steve Simpson (mathematician)|url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/288374692 |title=Subsystems of second order arithmetic |date=2009 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |others=Association for Symbolic Logic |isbn=978-0-521-88439-6 |edition=2nd |series=Perspectives in logic |location=Cambridge; New York |oclc=288374692}}</ref><sup>p.&nbsp;243</sup> Every β-model of second-order arithmetic is also an ω-model, since working within the model we can prove that &lt; is a well-ordering, so &lt; really is a well-ordering of the [[Natural number|natural numbers]] of the model.<ref name="AM" />

There is an incompleteness theorem for β-models: if T is a recursively axiomatizable theory in the language of second-order arithmetic, analogously to how there is a model of T+"there is no model of T" if there is a model of T, there is a β-model of T+"there are no countable coded β-models of T" if there is a β-model of T. A similar theorem holds for β<sub>n</sub>-models{{clarify|date=April 2026}} for any natural number <math>n\geq 1</math>.<ref>C. Mummert, S. G. Simpson, "[https://sgslogic.net/t20/papers/betan.pdf An Incompleteness Theorem for β<sub>n</sub>-Models]", 2004. Accessed 22 October 2023.</ref>

Axioms based on β-models provide a natural finer division of the strengths of subsystems of second-order arithmetic, and also provide a way to formulate reflection principles. For example, over <math>\mathsf{ATR}_0</math>, <math>\Pi^1_1\mathsf{-CA}_0</math> is equivalent to the statement "for all <math>X</math> [of second-order sort], there exists a countable β-model ''M'' such that <math>X\in M</math>.<ref name="Simpson2009" /><sup>p.&nbsp;253</sup> (Countable ω-models are represented by their sets of integers, and their satisfaction is formalizable in the language of analysis by an inductive definition.) Also, the theory extending KP with a canonical [[axiom schema]] for a recursively Mahlo universe (often called <math>KPM</math>)<ref>M. Rathjen, [https://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~rathjen/KPM-Ordinal-Analysis.pdf Proof theoretic analysis of KPM] (1991), p.381. Archive for Mathematical Logic, Springer-Verlag. Accessed 28 February 2023.</ref> is logically equivalent to the theory Δ{{su|b=2|p=1}}-CA+BI+(Every true Π{{su|b=3|p=1}}-formula is satisfied by a β-model of Δ{{su|b=2|p=1}}-CA).<ref>M. Rathjen, [https://www1.maths.leeds.ac.uk/~rathjen/BEYOND.pdf Admissible proof theory and beyond], Logic, Methodology and Philosophy of Science IX (Elsevier, 1994). Accessed 2022-12-04.</ref>

Additionally, <math>\mathsf{ACA}_0</math> proves a connection between β-models and the hyperjump: for all sets <math>X</math> of integers, <math>X</math> has a hyperjump iff there exists a countable β-model <math>M</math> such that <math>X\in M</math>.<ref name="Simpson2009" /><sup>p.&nbsp;251</sup>

Every β-model of comprehension is elementarily equivalent to an ω-model which is not a β-model.<ref>A. Mostowski, Y. Suzuki, "[https://eudml.org/doc/214123 On ω-models which are not β-models]". Fundamenta Mathematicae vol. 65, iss. 1 (1969).</ref>

==In set theory==
A notion of β-model can be defined for models of second-order set theories (such as Morse-Kelley [[set theory]]) as a model <math>(M, \mathcal X)</math> such that the membership relations of <math>(M, \mathcal X)</math> is well-founded, and for any relation <math>R\in\mathcal X</math>, <math>(M, \mathcal X)\vDash</math>"<math>R</math> is well-founded" iff <math>R</math> is in fact well-founded. While there is no least transitive model of MK, there is a least β-model of MK.<ref>K. J. Williams, "[https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.09526.pdf The Structure of Models of Second-order Set Theories]", PhD thesis, 2018.</ref><sup>pp.&nbsp;17,154–156</sup>
